title: Immunity & vaccines
examples: How does my body know what to fight off?
What is the difference between natural and artificial immunity?

explain.say: Today we are learning about how your body fights sickness.

items: Immunity is the body's defence system.
It fights off germs called pathogens.
It keeps you healthy from getting sick.

explain.say: First, your body uses phagocytes to eat germs.
Next, your body makes antibodies to target specific invaders.
Then, memory cells remember the germ for future attacks.
Vaccines introduce weak germs to build memory cells safely.
When you get a vaccine, it is like a practice drill for your body.

faq.q: How long do memory cells last in my body?
faq.a: Memory cells can remain in your body for many years. They wait for the specific germ to return. You might also ask: How long does immunity last? Or: Do vaccines make permanent protection?
asks: How long do memory cells last?

faq.q: What exactly are antibodies made of?
faq.a: Antibodies are specialized proteins made by your immune system. They have a unique shape that fits only one type of germ. You could also ask: What is the structure of an antibody? Or: Are antibodies proteins?
asks: What is the structure of an antibody?

faq.q: If I get sick from a germ, does that build immunity?
faq.a: Yes, getting sick and recovering can build immunity. However, this is often riskier than vaccination. You might also ask: Is natural infection enough? Or: Can I get immunity from illness?
asks: Can I get immunity from illness?

faq.q: Are all germs that cause sickness covered by vaccines?
faq.a: No, vaccines cover specific, known pathogens. Scientists are always working to develop vaccines for new threats. You might also ask: Is there a vaccine for everything? Or: Are there gaps in vaccine coverage?
asks: Are all germs covered by vaccines?
Is there a vaccine for everything?
Are there gaps in vaccine coverage?

faq.q: What is the role of phagocytes in fighting infection?
faq.a: Phagocytes act like clean-up crews, physically engulfing and digesting pathogens. They are the first line of defence when germs enter the body. You could also ask: What do phagocytes do? Or: How do phagocytes fight germs?
asks: Are phagocytes like white blood cells?

facts: Phagocytes are cells that engulf and digest pathogens.
Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins specific to certain antigens.
Memory cells allow for a faster response upon re-exposure.
Vaccines introduce weakened or dead pathogens safely.

quiz.say: What is the primary function of phagocytes?
quiz.why: Phagocytes are specialized cells whose job is to physically eat and break down invading germs.

wrong.0: This is the job of plasma cells, not the phagocytes themselves.
wrong.1: Memory cell creation happens after the initial immune response.
wrong.2: While they help clean up, their main action is physical engulfment.

quiz.say: If a person receives a vaccine, what component is usually introduced?

options.show: A strong dose of antibodies immediately.
options.say: A strong dose of antibodies immediately.

options.show: A weakened or inactive form of the pathogen.
options.say: A weakened or inactive form of the pathogen.

quiz.why: Vaccines use parts of germs that cannot make you sick but teach your body how to fight them.

wrong.0: The goal is to teach the body to make antibodies, not just give them.
wrong.1: While boosters exist, the initial vaccine uses germ components.
wrong.3: Giving the full active germ would make the person very sick.

quiz.say: A person is exposed to Germ X. After recovery, their body has high levels of specific antibodies and memory cells. This shows:
quiz.why: Acquired immunity means the body learned how to fight the germ through exposure or vaccination.

wrong.0: This scenario describes immunity gained through vaccination as well.
wrong.2: Innate immunity is the immediate, non-specific first line of defence.
wrong.3: Passive immunity comes from receiving ready-made antibodies from another source.
